title: How I automated sports market research with an AI agent, without handing it my wallet (and it places the trade too)
author: Dry-Comfortable-2678
selftext:
Researching one game used to mean a dozen tabs: injury reports, recent form, head-to-head, the line, how much liquidity was actually behind it. I’d form a view, then lose it by the time I’d checked the price again. None of that research was saved anywhere, so I couldn’t tell later whether I’d been right for the right reasons.

The video is the whole loop in six prompts: find the games that matter, build a thesis, find the trade, size it, execute and manage it, then scan for probability gaps.

Today all of that lives in one place, and I drive it with an AI agent. I ask in plain English, like “what sports markets should I be watching today?” It pulls the schedule, injuries, form, head-to-head and live market prices, then compares its own estimate to what the market is pricing. Every market pays $1 if the outcome happens, so a team at 39¢ is a 39% chance, and the agent’s job is to find where it disagrees and say why.

How the AI part works: the agent has its own wallet, separate from mine, and runs inside a policy I set: a max per trade and a daily cap. In the video it’s $100 per trade and $250 a day. On my own wallet I run $10 and $25. The caps are enforced in code before anything executes, so the model can suggest anything but the policy decides what runs. Every trade starts as a preview showing effective price, price impact, fee and remaining cap, and nothing happens until I confirm. After a fill it proposes an exit rule, like take profit at 65¢ or stop under 40¢, and only arms it if I approve.

The last prompt in the video checked fifteen markets and ranked the five widest gaps. The biggest was the Raiders at 39¢ against its 48% estimate, because it thinks the market is still pricing New England as last year’s team. Then it placed nothing. Its reasoning was that gaps narrow as injury reports land and pools deepen before game day, so it flagged them and said it would alert me if any widened past 10 points. That’s what I want from an agent touching money: most of the time, the right answer is no trade.

Then I kept adding the things I’d want as a trader:

* Moneylines across NFL, NBA, WNBA, MLB, NHL, college football and basketball, UFC, boxing, NASCAR and golf
* A probability chart per game with events marked on it (kickoff, period changes, injury reports), so you can see what moved the line
* A daily brief: wallet balance, open positions and P&L, track record, and the games worth a look
* Combos across games
* Free built-in data for schedules, injuries, form, head-to-head, gaps and liquidity

Results so far, small sample: 8 settled trades from my own agent wallet, 5 wins and 3 losses, +$41.25 realized, all inside the $10 cap. That proves nothing yet. I’ll keep posting the record as it grows, losses included.

Stack is Claude for reasoning, Circle Agent Wallets for the agent’s wallet, YES and NO outcome tokens backed by USDC, and settlement on Arc. 

What it doesn’t do (yet): it can’t prove it’s calibrated. When it says 48%, it needs to be right about 48% of the time, and that takes far more settled markets than I have. It’s also only as good as its news timing. A questionable tag thirty minutes before kickoff can flip the read. And a real gap isn’t worth much in a thin pool, which is why liquidity sits next to every gap.

It uses real USDC on Arc, with a 1 USDC minimum, 18+. I’m looking for testers, especially anyone already trading on Polymarket or Kalshi.

Two real questions for you:

Would you let an agent execute inside hard caps, or keep it on research only? And what would you want to see in its track record before trusting its probabilities?

  
App: [https://www.mantua.ai/](https://www.mantua.ai/)

Disclosure: I’m the founder. Criticism welcome, especially on how it estimates probabilities.

Hope it helps someone do their research faster.
